Introduction - October 2010 











##### **Introduction** 

With the metals industry gathering in London for LME Week, it is an ideal time to review the events of the last twelve months and, more importantly, assess the prospects for 2011.  GFMS have extended its supply-demand and balance forecasts out to 2011 on both an annual and quarterly basis. We have also reviewed our projections for the rest of 2010. 

example is nickel, where despite a 30% increase in stainless output, nickel consumption fell by around 13%.  The good new

s for base metal producers is that this has largely come to an end and we are looking for a return of strong apparent consumption growth in 2011 from China. 

###### **Chinese growth and energy consumption** 

Comparing the LME official cash price on 6th October with that a year earlier, all the metals have registered gains. Tin registered the largest increase with a 78.4% rise.  The GFMS’ Base Metals Index, which gives equal weight to the six non-ferrous metals, rose by 33.1% over this period to 334.40, marking a year-to-date peak.  The low over the last twelve months was recorded at 231.84 on June 8. 

###### **What will be the market drivers in 2011?** 

A number of key features have emerged since the previous LME Week.  First, was the rapid rebound in demand in the mature economies.  This obviously reflected the exceptionally low base, the earlier stimulus packages and the various industry-specific measures.  As a result, year-onyear demand growth in some of these countries at over 30% has outstripped that of China so far this year - a move that we do not expect to be repeated.  Our forecasts see a return towards trend growth, which means limited expansion in mature economies’ demand.  On an end-use basis, we may see some growth in demand from sectors that have lagged behind so far in the recovery, such as construction. 

As discussed in the next section, concerns about the sustainability of rapid economic expansion in China appear to have evaporated.  This suggests that underlying demand in China  should remain strong.  Another factor relating to the Chinese non-ferrous metals sector are the recent attempts to limit energy consumption to meet targets under the Eleventh 5-year Plan, which finished at the end of September.  Data is not yet available on the impact on non-ferrous production, and we only expect fairly limited declines.  Also it is still not clear whether the emergency measures will be extended. Given these measures will affect primary output more than downstream activity this can be viewed as a fairly positive (if temporary) factor for the broader LME metals sector. 

Other sources of strong projected demand growth include the other BRICs, particularly from India and Brazil.  It should be noted that these countries generally account for between 6-9% of global demand.  2010 has seen a sharp rebound in South Korea and to a less extent Taiwan.  Although consumption growth will slow, the metals sector will continue to benefit from firm export demand in the region.  We are also fairly positive about the trends for the ASEAN nations. 

###### **When will Chinese destocking end?** 

In contrast to the mature economies, where there was some inevitable restocking as downstream production recovered, there has been destocking of a number of metals in China in response to the surge in inventories that were built up in 2009.  This is reflected in the apparent consumption figures so far this year, that have been well behind downstream output (

rb production from a wide variety of sources, which removes some of the risk of the timing on certain projects slipping. For aluminium, despite recent cutbacks in China, we continue to view these as mostly temporary and there is still capacity in the pipeline within the country to replace the closure of any small scale polluting smelters. In addition there is new production from the Middle East and India to be absorbed. ###### **Price prospects** Once again, the traditional inverse relationship between inventories and prices has not been in much evidence. Many of the aspects that have boosted the role of funds in base metals (and commodities generally) remain place so there is the potential for prices to once again ignore stock increases and post further gains. For all the base metals, GFMS is forecasting higher average annual prices in 2011 than in 2010. However, the extent of the increases will vary significantly. Also importantly, it should be remembered that prices will not go up in a straight line. We see two obvious opportunities for a correction in prices. One may come post LME Week when it becomes clear that the physical market is not be quite as tight as suggested by the run up in prices. The second factor that in our view will trigger a correction is based on the mediumterm fundamentals. GFMS expects that economic growth will slow in the early part of next year as the impact of the switch to fiscal tightening becomes clear. We have already seen the downside potential for base metal prices on the back of concerns about economic growth earlier this year. As noted earlier we have amended our projections. For our new base and alternative scenarios for supply-demand and price see the individual sections. Its manufacturing index fell to 54.4 in September from 56.3 in August, which represents the fourth fall in the last five months. Importantly, new orders declined by 2 points to 51.1. Although the index may stay above the critical 50 level, it seem inevitable that activity will slow, particularly as inventories are rising. Another closely watched indicator is the University of Michigan consumer sentiment index, which dipped by 0.7 in September. The index remains well below the level seen in the first half of the year. There are a number of reasons behind the fall including an uptick in the unemployment rate, and continued uncertainty about policy. The survey shows that consumers expectations about future prospects remain weak. There is still little sign of improvement in the key construction sector. New home sales in August were at a seasonally adjusted annualised rate (SAAR) of 288,000, a record low. As we have seen in a number of countries, low interest rates are not a sufficient catalyst to encourage buyers back into the market. The debt overhang remains and fears of a double-dip, or even just a period of slower growth are keeping buyers on the sidelines. The Eurozone economic sentiment index is showing slightly surprising signs of strength.  It registered its fourth increase in a row in September rising to 103.2.  However, the sovereign debt issue has yet to go away, while fiscal tightening measures that are in place will begin to kick-in. This is imposed on an already weak employment situation. 

The influential quarterly Tankan survey of large Japanese enterprises has just been released.  The index increased from 1 to 8 continuing the recovery from depths of -60 in the first quarter of 2009.  The survey results for the non-ferrous 

and other commodity sectors were more buoyant, but these largely reflect the better global conditions for the markets. Some other aspects of the survey were less encouraging for the base metal producers.  For example, construction sector sentiment remained firmly in negative territory at -21. 

The data from China remains more reassuring for the base metals sector.  The industrial production and fixed asset investment data released in the middle of September was supportive  coming in at 13.9% and 24% year-on-year growth respectively.  More recently, the September PMI data, which showed an increase to 52.9 from 51.9 in August, further allayed fears of a slowdown in the rate of economic growth.

We forecast a fourth quarter average price of $7,950/tonne, resulting in a full year average of $7,350/ tonne._** - **_Weaker supply-demand conditions are projected for the first half of next year, as a slow-down in global economic growth affects consumption. A short-lived return to oversupply, albeit modest, is likely._** - **_Although lower than in the current quarter, prices are expected to remain far higher than marginal costs of production._** - **_As many of the problems faced by the global economy are shaken off later in the year, we project a return to deficits in the second half. Coupled with re

Source: GFMS Independent - Informed - International **C1** Copper - October 2010 ###### **Market background** The rally we noted in the early part of September held strong for the remainder of the month and through to the present time. Copper prices broke through a series of barriers unseen since April, by end-September breaking through the $8,000/tonne barrier on a sustainable basis and recently peaking above $8,300/tonne, on an intra-day basis, reaching levels unseen since July 2008. Ongoing positive results for the industrial sector around the world have continued to underpin prices. China continues to lead the pack, with solid double-digit growth in industrial production remaining undisturbed and its September PMI rising to 52.9 from 51.9 in August, calming some of the fears that the inevitable slow-down in the country could prove severe. In Europe, North America and Japan, despite ongoing concerns about the fragility of the recovery, to-date the manufacturing/industrial sector continues to demonstrate growth on a year-on-year basis. GFMS are convinced the fundamental market for copper is in deficit. Falling inventories, anecdotal information, healthy premia and longer-dated

futures prices in backwardation are all supportive of a tight spot market. Having said this, we do not believe that this tightness alone could have precipitated prices rocketing to current levels. Perhaps more important over the last few weeks has been the re-emergence of the quantitative easing thesis on the table for a number of monetary authorities around the world. Notably, throughout September, speculation that the Federal Reserve would enter a new round of loosening monetary policy, in the light of persistently disappointing growth, confirmed late in the month by the organisation, has put considerable pressure on the US dollar. In our view this has been the single most importantly driver of the rise noted across most commodity prices. Announcements suggesting other countries may well be following suit has further reduced the appeal of holding cash, boosting investment demand across most other asset classes, greatly benefiting copper. The speculator-driven nature of the recent rally in copper prices and the high correlation with other assets raises alarm bells towards the short term prospects for copper prices. Once the excitement of the forthcoming LME week passes, we would expect a noteworthy correction to take place, before a rising trend is resumed for much of the rest of the year. As we discuss in detail later in this section, GFMS have extended our forecast to the end of 2011. On the fundamental front, we continue to see temporary weakness emerge in the first half of the year, as another setback in the global economic recovery affects consumption, but we see prices keeping to relatively high levels. As the steadier sources of economic growth begin to gather momentum in the second half, we forecast a return to deficit conditions, fuelling a rally to all-time highs before the end of the year. ###### **LME stocks continue to fall** The decline of LME inventories continued throughout September and at end-month stocks stood below 374,000 tonnes, 24,000 tonnes lower than one month prior and 181,000 tonnes below their February peak. Reported stocks also fell in Shanghai, by 23,000 tonnes to their endSeptember level of around 87,000 tonnes. ###### **The Chinese market remains tight** We do not view the marginal decline suffered by semis production in August on the month-on-month basis as indicative of a trend but rather reflecting seasonality. A more relevant statistic to the state of local consumption in our view is the 15% year-on-year increase in the monthly figure, and the 18% rise in the year-to-date cumulative total. The latest figures from the central bank of Zambia show that production growth cont

inues in the country. Output in the first seven months of this year was 4,724 tonnes versus 2,534 tonnes in the corresponding period of 2009. Sales were up to 4,725 tonnes up from 2,521 tonnes. ###### **With further increases in the pipeline** In the nickel section, we highlight the additions to supply associated with revival of output at Vale’s Sudbury operation following the resolution of the strike. It also appears that the strike at the company’s Voisey’s Bay operation is finally reaching its conclusion. Vale is also in the process of ramping up its Goro project that could eventually yield 4,000 tpy of cobalt. Other contributors to extra cobalt production in 2011 should include Sherritt Gordon’s 5,600 tpy Ambatovey project. The company is planning for the project to be commissioned late in the first half of next year. The market will also have to absorb projects from the African cobalt-belt the largest of which is Tenke. QNI is looking for feed for its second production line at its Yabulu nickel refinery from the Ravensthorpe operation, which is owned by First Quantum Minerals. At its current capacity, the Yabulu plant produces 32,000 tpy of nickel and 2,000 tpy of cobalt Looking further ahead, the cobalt market is likely to have to absorb the Boleo copper-cobalt project, which is owned by Baja Mining. The project may be commissioned late 2012, with a cobalt capacity of around 1,600 tonnes. ###### **Market outlook** GFMS has re-assessed and extended its price projections out to 2011. Although we remain positive about the demand prospects for the metal, the market is having to cope with a surge in supply. So far this year the market has just about absorb the increase. However next year, even if some of the new projects in the pipeline do not quite come onstream as scheduled, we still believe that the cobalt market will return to surplus in 2011. This in turn should limit the increase to prices, which could see the high grade quote average $15.0/lb next year. ||**~~Quarterl~~**
